name: Euphoric recall
statement: Euphoric recall is the clinical claim that people who use drugs remember the pleasure of past use and lose the memory of its costs.
meaning: The term belongs to addiction counselling rather than to experimental psychology. Its claim is that memories of intoxication keep their pleasant content while the harm attached to the same episodes drops away, and that the surviving half pulls a person back towards use. Vernon E. Johnson's 'I'll Quit Tomorrow' places it beside blackouts and repression, which frames it as a defence of the drinking rather than as an ordinary quirk of memory. One Internet Archive catalogue record for the 1980 revised edition lists a chapter titled 'Blackouts, repression, and euphoric recall'. The book's text could not be obtained, so nothing about its argument is stated here. In the journals the phrase travels as a mechanism taken for granted. A review of art therapy and addiction says that 'a major hurdle in addiction treatment is reducing the euphoric recall of substances during withdrawal cravings that lead to relapse'. An article proposing a compulsive eating phenotype writes that 'this "euphoric recall" persists and encourages overeating even after food loses its appeal'. Neither is a study of the thing named. No operational definition was located: no rating scale, no comparison condition, and no published measure.

origin.where: I'll Quit Tomorrow, revised edition, Harper & Row
origin.note: No source claiming to have coined the phrase was located. The earliest dated use found is the chapter title 'Blackouts, repression, and euphoric recall'. It appears in the contents note of one Internet Archive catalogue record for the 1980 revised edition, 182 pages. Two further Internet Archive items for that edition carry no contents note at all, so the chapter title rests on a single record. Open Library records a first edition of 1973 at 168 pages, and the Internet Archive holds a scan of it. That scan is lending restricted, its plain text answers HTTP 401, and its search inside route answers 403 with a page headed 'Item not available'. The 1973 edition therefore could not be searched, and the phrase may be older than the year given here. On 21 September 2026 the Internet Archive full-text hosts failed at this session's proxy with a 502 on connect. HathiTrust full-text search answered a Cloudflare challenge under a 403, and the Google Books API returned 429 for exceeded daily quota. So no earlier print use could be searched for in books.

evidence: No study measuring euphoric recall was located. The clinical sources make the claim by description and offer no ratings, no control condition and no comparison against what people said at the time. The nearest measured work sits one step away and asks a different question. Carter and Tiffany's meta-analysis of 41 cue-reactivity studies compared responses of alcoholics, cigarette smokers, cocaine addicts and heroin addicts to drug-related against neutral stimuli. Across all groups the effect size for self-reported craving was +0.92. Alcoholics gave a significantly smaller craving effect size of +0.53 against +1.18 to +1.29 for the other groups. The physiological effect sizes were smaller again, and the abstract gives them across all groups rather than for alcoholics alone: heart rate +0.26, sweat gland activity +0.40, skin temperature -0.24. Those figures are read from the structured abstract at Europe PMC, and they measure craving elicited by a cue, not the content of a remembered episode. The nearest theoretical treatment is Bornstein and Pickard's review in Neuropsychopharmacology, which proposes that drug choices are biased by selective sampling of individual episodic memories at the moment of decision. It is a framework paper reporting no new data, it takes its title from addiction folklore rather than from a measurement, and the word euphoric does not appear anywhere in its text as searched for this entry. Its own statement of the position is that despite evidence linking the hippocampus to addiction-related behaviours, 'the role of memory retrieval remains less well-understood, and potentially crucial'.

examples.tag: The night that comes back in pieces
examples.text: Someone giving up drinking thinks back to an evening in the pub and reaches the warmth and the company first. The sickness of the next morning belongs to the same evening and does not arrive with the rest of it.

Walking past a familiar shop brings back the ease the first drink used to give, while the arguments that followed stay out of view. The half of the memory that survives is the half that pulls towards use.

examples.tag: Telling the story of a bad year
examples.text: A man in treatment retells a period of heavy use as a run of funny episodes, and the debt and the lost job sit outside the telling. He is not lying. The costs are simply not what the memory hands back.

replication.headline: Nothing was found to replicate. Euphoric recall is a piece of clinical vocabulary with a long life in treatment settings and no experiment behind it that this search could find.
replication.detail: Europe PMC returns six records for the phrase, and all six use it in passing: a compulsive eating brief report, an art therapy review, a philosophy of technology paper on personalised language models, a 2009 Mayo Clinic Proceedings correspondence reply on relapse in anaesthesia staff, a review of mirtazapine as pharmacotherapy, and a conference abstract book. A search of Europe PMC titles and abstracts for the phrase returns nothing. PubMed and NCBI Bookshelf both report the quoted phrase as not found in their indexes. Crossref returns no work whose title carries it and arXiv returns none. The APA Dictionary of Psychology offers no term beginning euphoric, and its five entries beginning recall do not include this one. Every one of those searches was run again on 21 September 2026 and returned the same result. The nearest measured relatives are drug-cue reactivity and the fading affect bias, entry 210, and both are different claims. Cue reactivity measures craving and arousal provoked by drug stimuli. The fading affect bias compares the emotion felt at an autobiographical event with the emotion felt on recalling it, across pleasant and unpleasant events, in general samples. Euphoric recall is a claim about what survives in the memory of a drug episode, made about dependent users. Treating the numbers from either literature as a measurement of it would be the error this entry warns about.

limits: The search covered Europe PMC by phrase and by title and abstract field, PubMed, NCBI Bookshelf, Crossref by title and by bibliographic query, arXiv, the Internet Archive item index, Open Library, and general web search, last on 21 September 2026. Four indexes refused the request on that day. OpenAlex answered 429 because the free daily budget shared by this session's egress address was spent. Semantic Scholar answered 429 on two attempts, the Google Books API answered 429 for exceeded daily quota, and HathiTrust full-text search answered a Cloudflare challenge under a 403. The Internet Archive full-text hosts failed at the proxy with a 502 on connect and scholar.archive.org was rate limited. Only the English phrase was searched. None of the books that carry the concept was obtained: Johnson, and the works by Perkinson, Gorski, Keane, Washton and Zweben, and the Daley volume that the Wikipedia article cites. The Internet Archive holds scans of Johnson and of Perkinson, and both are lending restricted and answer HTTP 401 to the text. Of the three journal items named by that article, one was obtained here. Neighbors and colleagues on cognitive factors in addiction is open at PubMed Central, and the word euphoric does not appear anywhere in it. Hammersley's 1994 digest in Addiction and Brown's 2000 paper in the Journal of Psychoactive Drugs are recorded closed at Unpaywall and have no Wayback capture, so only their abstracts were read. Brown's abstract describes focus groups with professional substance abuse counsellors, and Hammersley's describes a review of the limits of self-report. Neither abstract reports a measure of euphoric recall, and neither full text was seen. So this entry cannot say who coined the phrase or when it first reached print. An absence of evidence found by this search is not evidence that the clinicians are describing nothing.
misreadings: The first error is inherited from the lists. Euphoric recall sits in Wikipedia's catalogue of cognitive biases among entries that carry experiments, which invites a reader to expect an effect size, and none was located. Its bullet there carries no reference, while the bullets on either side of it do. The second is conflation with the measured memory effects nearby. Rosy retrospection, entry 81, compares evaluations of an event made before, during and after it. The fading affect bias, entry 210, compares the emotion at an event with the emotion at recall, and the finding is that unpleasant affect fades faster than pleasant affect. Euphoric recall is a claim about drug memories specifically, and about pleasant content being kept while harm is dropped, which is neither of those comparisons. The third error is citation drift, and it runs in two places. Giubilini and four colleagues, writing in Science and Engineering Ethics, list 'the euphoric recall and negativity biases' and cite for both a chapter by Unkelbach, Alves and Koch whose title names negativity bias, positivity bias and valence asymmetries. That chapter was not obtained here, so this entry says only where the citation points. Wikipedia does the same thing in its theoretical framework, citing Neighbors and colleagues for the expectancy account of euphoric recall. That paper was read in full here and never uses the phrase. The last error is to read clinical currency as evidence. The phrase has been in treatment vocabulary since at least 1980 and is used in peer-reviewed articles as an accepted mechanism, and neither fact is a measurement.

sources.text: Internet Archive catalogue record for Johnson, V. E., I'll Quit Tomorrow, San Francisco: Harper & Row, 1980, 182 pages. Its contents note lists the chapter 'Blackouts, repression, and euphoric recall'. This is the only one of the three Internet Archive items for that edition to carry a contents note; the other two carry none. The scan is lending restricted and the text was not obtained.

Open Library edition records for I'll Quit Tomorrow. Source for the first edition of 1973 at 168 pages, Harper & Row, and for the 1980 revised edition at 182 pages. The 1973 edition is scanned at the Internet Archive as illquittomorrow00john_0, which is lending restricted and answered HTTP 401 to its text on 21 September 2026.

Carter, B. L., & Tiffany, S. T. (1999). Meta-analysis of cue-reactivity in addiction research. Addiction, 94(3), 327-340. The effect sizes quoted here are read from the structured abstract at Europe PMC. The full text was not obtained: Wiley answers a Cloudflare challenge rather than a paywall notice, Unpaywall records the article closed, and the one Wayback capture of the landing page carries the abstract only.

Bornstein, A. M., & Pickard, H. (2020). 'Chasing the first high': memory sampling in drug choice. Neuropsychopharmacology, 45(6), 907-915. Read in full at PubMed Central. The nearest peer-reviewed treatment of the idea, and the source for the memory sampling framework described above.

Quinn, P. (2024). Art therapy's engagement of brain networks for enduring recovery from addiction. Frontiers in Psychiatry, 15, article 1458063. Europe PMC records the publication year as 2024 and Crossref dates it 6 January 2025. Read in full at Europe PMC. Quoted as an instance of the phrase used in a journal as a settled mechanism.

Tarman, V. I. (2025). Volume addiction: introducing a novel phenotype within compulsive high volume eating. Frontiers in Public Health, 13, article 1760037. Read in full at Europe PMC, which types it a brief report. Europe PMC records the publication year as 2025 and Crossref dates it 12 January 2026. Quoted as an instance of the phrase carried across to eating.

Giubilini, A., Porsdam Mann, S., Voinea, C., Earp, B., & Savulescu, J. (2024). Know thyself, improve thyself: personalized LLMs for self-knowledge and moral enhancement. Science and Engineering Ethics, 30(6), article 54. Read in full at Europe PMC. The source for the citation drift described above.

Unkelbach, C., Alves, H., & Koch, A. (2020). Negativity bias, positivity bias, and valence asymmetries: explaining the differential processing of positive and negative information. Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 62, 115-187. Crossref carries the title and the page range but no authors and no volume, so the authors and the volume are taken from the Cologne repository record, which holds no full text. Not obtained; cited only as the work the preceding article points to.

Neighbors, C., Tomkins, M. M., Lembo Riggs, J., Angosta, J., & Weinstein, A. P. (2019). Cognitive factors and addiction. Current Opinion in Psychology, 30, 128-133. Read in full at PubMed Central on 21 September 2026. Wikipedia cites it for the expectancy account of euphoric recall, and the word euphoric does not appear in it.

Brown, N. K. (2000). Clinical judgments of high-risk behavior during recovery. Journal of Psychoactive Drugs, 32(3), 299-304. Abstract only, read at Europe PMC; the full text is recorded closed at Unpaywall and has no Wayback capture. The abstract describes focus groups with professional substance abuse counsellors and reports no measure of euphoric recall.

Hammersley, R. (1994). A digest of memory phenomena for addiction research. Addiction, 89(3), 283-293. Abstract only, read at Europe PMC; the full text is recorded closed at Unpaywall and has no Wayback capture. The abstract describes a review of the limits of self-report in addiction research.

Wikipedia, 'Euphoric recall', wikitext read on 21 September 2026, and 'List of cognitive biases', wikitext read the same day. Used to find the books and papers named in the limits above, and cited as the object of the list problem described in misreadings, not as evidence for anything.
